source_title: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions
baselines_compared: A capabilities-only fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo (same recipe minus hierarchy data), and that baseline augmented with a prompted system message spelling out the hierarchy; the trained hierarchy substantially outperforms the prompting baseline.
key_result: Fine-tuning GPT-3.5 Turbo on synthetic instruction-hierarchy data improves robustness on every safety evaluation, with defense against system-prompt extraction improving by 63% over the capabilities-only baseline. Gains generalize to attack classes deliberately held out of training (jailbreaks, password extraction, injection via tool use) by up to 34%, with jailbreak robustness up over 30%, while TriviaQA/LAMBADA/HellaSwag capability scores are comparable to baseline.
technical_summary: Proposes the instruction hierarchy, an explicit privilege ordering over System Messages, User Messages, Model Outputs and Tool Outputs, so the model treats lower-privileged text as data rather than commands whenever the two conflict. Builds training data two ways: decomposing compositional benign requests into aligned sub-instructions placed lower in the hierarchy via context distillation, and using red-teamer LLMs to synthesize misaligned instructions the model is trained to answer as if it never saw them; it then fine-tunes GPT-3.5 Turbo with SFT and RLHF. Evaluates on open-source and novel benchmarks covering direct injection, indirect injection via browsing and tools, system-prompt extraction, jailbreaks and over-refusal, deliberately holding out several attack classes to test generalization. Matters because it reframes prompt injection as a missing privilege abstraction rather than a filtering problem, and is the deployed training-time defense that later alignment-based defenses such as StruQ and SecAlign position themselves against.
datasets_benchmarks: TensorTrust Prompt Hijacking and TensorTrust Robustness/password extraction (Toyer et al.); Gandalf Game password extraction (Lakera AI); jailbreakchat.com jailbreaks with unsafe and with allowed prompts; known ChatGPT jailbreaks; author-created held-out synthetic sets for closed-domain direct injection, user conflicting/non-conflicting instructions, indirect injection via browsing, indirect injection via tool return values, system-prompt probing questions and borderline allowed prompts; capability checks on TriviaQA, LAMBADA, HellaSwag. Dataset sizes are not stated.

source_title: StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries
baselines_compared: Undefended instruction-tuned Llama and Mistral; test-time prompt defenses summarized by Liu et al. (Reminder in Prompt at 83% ASR, reminder after data, and other defensive prompts/delimiters, versus 96% undefended); and the training-time defenses BIPIA (reproduced with its official code on Vicuna-7B) and Jatmo (discussed as a different single-task scenario).
key_result: Structured instruction tuning drives the success rate of every tested manual prompt injection to under 2% on both Llama-7B and Mistral-7B (e.g., Completion-Real falls from 96% to 0% on Llama), with negligible utility cost (no significant AlpacaEval change on Llama, about one point on Mistral). It also generalizes to optimization-based attacks never seen in training, cutting TAP from 97% to 9% and GCG from 97% to 58%, and beats BIPIA, which leaves Completion-Real at 23% and GCG at 100%.
technical_summary: Proposes structured queries, which split an LLM call into separate prompt and data channels so the model is only ever permitted to take instructions from the prompt channel. Implements this as StruQ: a secure front-end that encodes prompt and data with reserved special delimiter tokens and filters those delimiters out of attacker-controlled data, plus structured instruction tuning that converts a base non-instruction-tuned LLM into one trained on a dataset augmented with injected-instruction examples whose target responses ignore the injection. Evaluates on 15+ attack types including the first prompt-injection evaluations with TAP and GCG, measuring utility with AlpacaEval, and compares against test-time prompt defenses and the training-time defense BIPIA. Matters because it is the reference fine-tuning-based separation defense whose failure modes under optimization-based and adaptive attacks later papers (SecAlign, adaptive-attack studies) build on directly.
datasets_benchmarks: Cleaned Alpaca instruction-tuning dataset for training; AlpacaEval 1.0 (GPT-4 judged win rate vs davinci003) for utility; an author-assembled suite of at least 15 prompt-injection attack types (Naive, Ignore, Escape-Deletion, Escape-Separation, Completion-Real/Other/Close and combined variants, plus TAP and GCG); 20 sub-sampled successful level-1 injections from the HackAPrompt competition dataset; BIPIA's test set of 231 prompt-injectable samples over email, table and WebQA.

source_title: Benchmarking and Defending against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models
baselines_compared: Undefended versions of the same LLMs, plus an ablation removing each defense component (explicit reminder; boundary awareness via in-context examples, border strings, datamarking, multi-turn separation, and special tokens plus adversarial training) and a comparison of three benign-response construction methods for the adversarial training set.
key_result: All 25 evaluated LLMs are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection on BIPIA, and more capable models (higher Arena Elo, e.g., GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-Turbo) tend to have higher attack success rates. The proposed black-box prompt-level defenses substantially reduce ASR but do not make models robust, while the white-box defense (special <data>/</data> boundary tokens plus adversarial fine-tuning) cuts ASR to nearly zero, roughly 10 times lower than the original ASR, with little loss in ROUGE or MT-Bench capability scores.
technical_summary: Introduces BIPIA, the first dedicated benchmark for indirect prompt injection, covering five real-world application scenarios and 50 attack types with instructions planted at varying positions inside external content, and uses it to show all 25 evaluated LLMs are vulnerable. Diagnoses two root causes -- LLMs cannot separate informational context from actionable instructions, and they lack awareness that instructions inside external content should not be executed -- and proposes matching defenses: black-box prompt-learning methods (explicit reminder, border strings and datamarking, in-context examples, multi-turn separation) and a white-box method that adds dedicated <data>/</data> tokens to the vocabulary and adversarially fine-tunes the model to answer correctly despite injections. Reports that only the white-box defense reaches near-zero ASR while preserving ROUGE and MT-Bench quality. Matters because BIPIA became a standard indirect-injection benchmark and a reproduced training-time baseline for later defenses such as StruQ.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces BIPIA: five application scenarios (email QA from 100 OpenAI Evals emails, web QA from 1,000 NewsQA examples, table QA from 1,000 WikiTableQuestions examples, summarization from 1,000 XSum examples, code QA from 100 Stack Overflow Python samples), 30 text and 20 code attack types with five malicious instructions each (250 attacker goals), injected at the beginning, middle or end of the external content, giving 626,250 training and 86,250 test prompts. Utility measured with ROUGE and MT-Bench.

source_title: Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting
baselines_compared: No-defense baseline ASR per model and task; a naive system-prompt instruction telling the model not to follow document instructions; and plain delimiting, against which the paper's datamarking and encoding variants are compared.
key_result: Spotlighting reduces attack success rate from above 50% to below 2% on GPT-family models with minimal task-efficacy loss. Concretely, a system-prompt warning alone has negligible effect and special delimiters only halve ASR, while datamarking takes GPT-3.5-Turbo from roughly 50% to below 3% (3.10%, and 8.0% in another task setting), GPT-4 to 1.0% and text-davinci-003 to 0.00%; encoding does even better, reaching 0.0% on summarization and 1.8% on Q&A. Datamarking shows no measurable degradation on SQuAD, SuperGLUE WiC, BoolQ or IMDB.
technical_summary: Introduces spotlighting, a family of prompt-engineering transformations that give untrusted input a continuous, model-visible signal of provenance so the LLM can tell system instructions from third-party data. Describes three instantiations of increasing strength -- delimiting (wrapping the data in special markers), datamarking (interleaving a randomly chosen marker token between every word of the data), and encoding (base64 or similar one-way transforms the attacker cannot control) -- and evaluates each on a 1,000-document injection corpus across three GPT models and several tasks, plus four standard NLP benchmarks to measure utility cost. Argues via an in-band versus out-of-band signaling analogy that these are mitigations, not a structural fix. Matters because datamarking/spotlighting became a widely reused ingestion-side baseline that later benchmarks (including BIPIA and guardrail papers) evaluate against.
datasets_benchmarks: An author-generated synthetic corpus of 1,000 documents containing keyword-payload prompt injections, used across summarization and Q&A task settings; utility measured on SQuAD Q&A, SuperGLUE Word-in-Context, SuperGLUE BoolQ and IMDB Sentiment.

source_title: SecAlign: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Preference Optimization
baselines_compared: Three fine-tuning-based defenses (StruQ, BIPIA, Jatmo, plus instruction hierarchy measured indirectly through GPT-4o-mini at 1% ASR on Ignore) and five prompting-based defenses including the SOTA In-Context defense, all against undefended models.
key_result: SecAlign drives optimization-free prompt injection to a consistent 0% ASR and is the first defense to keep optimization-based ASR mostly under 10%, reducing it by more than 4x versus StruQ, while leaving AlpacaEval2 WinRate statistically unchanged (difference under 0.7%). Undefended open-weight models show over 50% ASR from optimization-free attacks and 89% and 97% under optimization; StruQ stops optimization-free attacks but still leaves 27% and 45% ASR under optimization, and SecAlign cuts these to 1% and 8%. StruQ also costs about 4.5% WinRate on Llama3-8B-Instruct where SecAlign costs none.
technical_summary: Proposes SecAlign, which reframes prompt-injection defense as a preference-optimization problem rather than supervised fine-tuning. Builds a preference dataset automatically from any public instruction-tuning set by formatting each sample with instruction/data/response delimiters, injecting a prompt into the data part, and pairing the desirable output (answering the legitimate instruction) with an undesirable output (answering the injection), then runs DPO-style preference optimization so the model learns a large log-probability margin between secure and insecure responses. Argues this fixes StruQ's weakness, which only maximizes the probability of the secure response without suppressing the insecure one, and shows the margin explains generalization to unseen optimization-based attacks. Matters because it is the strongest training-time prompt-injection defense in this corpus by measured ASR, and it was subsequently scaled to a 70B open-weight model with built-in injection defense.
datasets_benchmarks: Cleaned Alpaca instruction-tuning dataset to build the preference dataset; AlpacaFarm (805 samples, 208 with a data part) for utility and security evaluation; AlpacaEval2 WinRate against davinci003 for utility; attack suite of optimization-free injections (Ignore, Completion, Ignore-Completion) and optimization-based injections (GCG, AdvPrompter, NeuralExec), none of which appear in training.

source_title: Attention Tracker: Detecting Prompt Injection Attacks in LLMs
baselines_compared: Two trained DeBERTa-v3-based detectors (Protect AI detector and Meta Prompt-Guard), LLM-based self-assessment detection, and known-answer detection; the paper notes no training-based detector is robust across both datasets.
key_result: Tracking attention on the original instruction detects injections with AUROC gains of up to 3.1% on Open-Prompt-Injection and up to 10.0% on the deepset dataset over the best existing detector, and among training-free methods the average AUROC gain is 31.3% (OPI) and 20.9% (deepset) across all five models. The method needs zero training data from any prompt injection dataset, works on models as small as 1.5B, and adds no extra LLM inference because attention is read from the forward pass the system already performs.
technical_summary: Identifies the distraction effect: under prompt injection, a specific subset of attention heads (termed important heads) shift their attention at the last token away from the original instruction and toward the injected instruction, and the size of this shift tracks attack success rate. Proposes Attention Tracker, a training-free detector that first finds the important heads once per model using 30 LLM-generated random sentences plus a naive ignore-attack, then scores any test query by the total attention those heads pay to the instruction and rejects queries whose focus score falls below a threshold. Evaluates on two public injection benchmarks and five small-to-mid open LLMs against trained, LLM-based and known-answer detectors. Matters because it is a detection defense whose signal comes from model internals rather than surface text, so it generalizes across attack phrasings and adds essentially zero inference cost.
datasets_benchmarks: Open-Prompt-Injection benchmark (Liu et al.) and the test set of the deepset prompt injection dataset, both containing normal and attack data; AUROC is the reported metric.

defense_name: UNNAMED: P2SQL mitigations (DB permission hardening + query rewriting)
source_title: From Prompt Injections to SQL Injection Attacks: How Protected is Your LLM-Integrated Web Application?
baselines_compared: None - the comparison is between unprotected Langchain, prompt-hardening patches written by the authors, and each of their four defenses; no prior defense system is used as a baseline.
key_result: Unmodified Langchain (v0.0.189) chatbots are wholly vulnerable: an adversary with only chatbot access gains complete read/write access to the application database, and prompt-hardening patches proved fragile and bypassable. All seven attacks succeeded on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, PaLM 2, Llama 2 and Vicuna 1.3 for both chain and agent setups (with one attack not reproducible on GPT-4, which was the most resistant model), and indirect attacks succeeded by storing injected text in a product review that the chatbot later read. The four proposed defenses, working together, thwarted all identified attacks with only modest to negligible latency overhead, with the LLM guard's cost roughly constant in query size.
technical_summary: Presents the first study of prompt-to-SQL (P2SQL) injection, where a prompt injection into a Langchain-based web chatbot is converted by the middleware into attacker-controlled SQL executed against the application database. Characterizes seven concrete attack variants across both SQLDatabaseChain and SQL-agent configurations, including indirect attacks in which the payload is stored in ordinary application data (a product review) and fires when the chatbot later reads it, and shows all seven work across seven LLMs. Proposes and implements a complementary four-part defense portfolio as Langchain extensions -- database role/permission hardening, rewriting the LLM-generated SQL query, an auxiliary LLM guard that validates query results, and in-prompt preloading of the authorized user's data -- and evaluates effectiveness and overhead on a real e-commerce application. Matters because it is the clearest demonstration in this corpus that context poisoning crosses from text into a downstream execution surface, and its defenses act after generation rather than on the prompt.
datasets_benchmarks: No standard benchmark; the authors build a set of seven representative P2SQL attacks (U.1 drop tables, U.2 change records, U.3 dump table contents, RD.1/RD.2 bypassing prompt restrictions on writes and reads, RI.1/RI.2 indirect attacks via injected database content) and evaluate them on a real-world open-source e-commerce application extended with a Langchain chatbot, loaded with the Amazon Books Reviews dataset (212,404 books, 2,004,568 reviews).

source_title: System-Level Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks: An Information Flow Control Perspective
baselines_compared: A vanilla ReAct-based LLM system implemented in LangChain (for security ASR and functionality), and SecGPT, a prior compartmentalization-based defense (for functionality/execution-correctness and overhead comparison).
key_result: The f-secure LLM system achieves 0% Attack Success Rate across all four backbone models and both InjectAgent settings, versus a vanilla ReAct LangChain system's 51.6%/67.4% ASR (base/enhanced) on GPT-3.5 Turbo and 28.7%/44.5% on GPT-4 Turbo. On functionality benchmarks it matches or improves execution correctness over the vanilla system and substantially outperforms the prior defense SecGPT, which achieves only 26.44% execution correctness on GPT-3.5 Turbo multi-tool tasks versus much higher for f-secure.
technical_summary: Proposes the f-secure LLM system, a system-level defense that disaggregates an LLM agent into a hub planner and spoke executors and applies information flow control principles so the planner never sees information derived, directly or indirectly, from untrusted sources. Introduces a security label model over the flow of information, a structured executable planning format, and a formal security property called execution trace non-compromise, proving vanilla LLM systems violate it while f-secure systems satisfy it. Evaluates on the InjectAgent indirect-prompt-injection benchmark and three tool-usage functionality benchmarks across four backbone LLMs, showing 0% ASR against all tested attacks while matching or exceeding the functionality and outperforming the prior SecGPT defense. Matters as a formally-grounded, IFC-based system-level architecture that structurally blocks the planner from being influenced by tainted content, at the cost of leaving individual tool-executor compromise (when a tool LLM must directly process malicious content) unaddressed.
datasets_benchmarks: InjectAgent indirect-prompt-injection benchmark (direct-harm and data-stealing attacks, base and enhanced settings) for security evaluation; three LangChain-Benchmarks tool-usage suites (single-tool, multiple-tool/Typewriter, multiple-tool collaboration/Relation Data) for functionality and overhead evaluation.

source_title: Signed-Prompt: A New Approach to Prevent Prompt Injection Attacks Against LLM-Integrated Applications
baselines_compared: None - no prior defense (e.g., delimiters, dual-LLM, input/output filtering) is empirically re-implemented or measured for comparison; the paper only contrasts its own LLM-PE and LLM-FT variants against each other and discusses prior defenses qualitatively in the introduction.
key_result: The prompt-engineered encoder achieves 96.67-100% correct substitution of natural-language 'delete' phrasings across the four test groups, and both Signed-Prompt-adjusted LLMs (LLM-PE and LLM-FT) show 0% attacker success rate at getting the unsigned deletion command executed across all four groups, though LLM-FT's correctness rate on legitimate signed user commands is inconsistent (73.34-100%) due to limited fine-tuning quality.
technical_summary: Proposes Signed-Prompt, a defense that has an authorized user's application front-end 'sign' sensitive instructions by substituting them with rare, near-arbitrary tokens (e.g., replacing 'delete' with 'toeowx') before they reach the LLM, so an adjusted LLM only executes the formatted command when it recognizes the signed token and treats the unsigned natural-language original as inert content; unsigned instructions injected by third parties therefore cannot trigger the sensitive action. Implements the encoder via GPT-4 prompt engineering and the adjusted LLM via both prompt engineering (GPT-4) and fine-tuning (ChatGLM-6B), evaluating only the single sensitive command 'delete' across four phrasing-variety test groups on a small author-built dataset. Reports 0% attacker success at triggering the true deletion command in all tested conditions. Matters as an early, simple token-substitution instance of an ingestion-side prompt/data separation defense, but its evaluation is limited to one command, one tiny custom dataset, no adversarial or optimization-based attacks, and no comparison against established defense baselines.
datasets_benchmarks: An author-created 'Delete Command Dataset' covering four groups of test phrasings for the single command 'delete' (direct, multilingual, varied expression, implication-based), used to test the encoder's substitution accuracy and the two adjusted LLMs' correctness/attack-success rates; no external or standard benchmark is used.

defense_name: UNNAMED: IPI detection + post-detection removal pipeline
source_title: Can Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks Be Detected and Removed?
baselines_compared: Attack baselines: Naive, Ignore, Escape-Character, Fake-completion, Combined attacks. Defense baselines: prompt-engineering-based Sandwich and Instructional defenses, and the fine-tuning-based StruQ defense, all compared against the paper's own detection models and its segmentation/extraction removal methods and their combined filtering pipeline.
key_result: A trained DeBERTa detector plus a Qwen2-1.5B extraction/segmentation removal pipeline (combined as a 'filtering' defense) generally outperforms prior prompt-engineering defenses (Sandwich, Instructional) and the fine-tuning defense StruQ on the Inj-TriviaQA benchmark, though all methods trained only on the Naive attack generalize poorly to the Fake-completion attack; the extraction removal method achieves removal rates of at least 94.66% for tail-positioned injections (the most effective attack position) but drops to a maximum of 67.77% for head/middle positions, and existing off-the-shelf detectors (including instructed LLMs and open-source guard models) struggle to reliably detect indirect injections, especially with over-defense and position-generalization problems.
technical_summary: Investigates whether indirect prompt injection attacks embedded in externally retrieved documents can be detected and subsequently removed, rather than only prevented at generation time. Constructs two new benchmarks (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA) with diverse injected instructions at multiple positions, evaluates existing instructed-LLM and open-source detectors, trains custom detection models, and proposes two removal methods, a segmentation-removal approach that deletes document segments flagged as containing injections and an extraction-removal approach that trains a model to identify and excise the injected span. Combines the best detection and removal components into a unified filtering defense and shows it outperforms prior prompt-engineering (Sandwich, Instructional) and fine-tuning (StruQ) baselines on Inj-TriviaQA, while identifying persistent weaknesses around injection position and cross-attack generalization. Matters as a systematic empirical study specifically of the post-detection removal step for indirect injection, a stage prior work largely neglects in favor of detection or prevention alone.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces Inj-SQuAD and Inj-TriviaQA, two benchmarks of 900 samples each built from SQuAD and TriviaQA validation data with diverse injected instructions at head/middle/tail positions; also constructs dedicated detection and removal training datasets; attack baselines are Naive, Ignore, Escape-Character, Fake-completion and Combined attacks (from Perez & Ribeiro, Breitenbach et al., Willison, and Liu et al.).

source_title: PromptShield: Deployable Detection for Prompt Injection Attacks
baselines_compared: PromptGuard and other existing prompt-injection detection schemes evaluated at matched, extremely low FPR operating points (1%, 0.5%, 0.1%, 0.05%), plus an internal architecture comparison across DeBERTa, FLAN-T5 (small/base/large) and Llama-3 (1B/8B) variants fine-tuned on the same benchmark.
key_result: The PromptShield detector (best configuration) achieves 65.3% true positive rate at 0.1% false positive rate on the benchmark's evaluation split, versus only 9.4% TPR at the same FPR for the best prior detector (PromptGuard achieves 22.8% TPR at 2.9% FPR, dropping to 12.8% TPR when its FPR is reduced to a comparable low level); larger fine-tuned architectures (FLAN-T5-large, Llama-3.1-8B) substantially outperform smaller ones (FLAN-T5-small, Llama-3.2-1B) in the low-FPR regime, and DeBERTa-v3-base outperforms all prior schemes above 0.1% FPR.
technical_summary: Introduces PromptShield, a benchmark and accompanying fine-tuned detector for prompt injection, motivated by the observation that prior detectors are evaluated unrealistically and fail to achieve the extremely low false-positive rates required for deployment given the large volume of benign traffic. Defines a taxonomy separating conversational chatbot data (assumed injection-free) from application-structured data (where injections occur), curates a benchmark spanning multiple instruction-following datasets and published optimization-free injection techniques with a dedicated low-FPR evaluation regime, and fine-tunes several classifier architectures on it. Shows that careful data curation plus larger models yields a detector that vastly outperforms prior schemes (including PromptGuard) specifically in the low-FPR operating range that matters for real deployment. Matters as a benchmark that reframes prompt-injection detection evaluation around realistic base rates and as a concretely stronger detection-stage defense than prior published detectors, though it targets only detection (not removal/mitigation) and is explicitly not evaluated against adaptive or optimization-based attackers.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces the PromptShield benchmark, curated from Alpaca, databricks-dolly, natural-instructions and SPP instruction-following datasets plus IFEval for conversational-style benign data, combined with application-structured data and prompt injection attacks generated via multiple optimization-free injection techniques from the literature; includes a dedicated train/evaluation split and a taxonomy separating conversational data from application-structured data.

source_title: PIGuard: Prompt Injection Guardrail via Mitigating Overdefense for Free
baselines_compared: Fmops, Deepset, PromptGuard, LakeraGuard, LlamaGuard3, and ProtectAIv2 (the prior best open-source model) compared on malicious accuracy, benign accuracy, over-defense accuracy (via NotInject), average accuracy, and inference efficiency; an ablation isolating the contribution of data augmentation alone versus the full MOF training strategy is also reported.
key_result: State-of-the-art prompt guard models (including ProtectAIv2) suffer severe over-defense, with over-defense accuracy on NotInject falling below 60% (near random guessing at 50%). PIGuard, trained with the proposed Mitigating Over-defense for Free (MOF) strategy, achieves 83.48% average accuracy across malicious, benign, and over-defense dimensions, surpassing the best prior open-source model (ProtectAIv2) by 30.4% (30.8% in the efficiency-adjusted table), with an over-defense accuracy of 87.32%, benign accuracy of 85.74%, and strong malicious accuracy, while rivaling commercial LLMs like GPT-4o and maintaining lower inference overhead than guardrail-style approaches.
technical_summary: Identifies that existing prompt-injection guardrail models suffer from severe over-defense, falsely flagging benign inputs containing common injection trigger words (e.g., 'ignore') as malicious, and introduces NotInject, a 339-sample evaluation dataset systematically measuring this bias, showing state-of-the-art guard models' over-defense accuracy collapses to near-random levels. Proposes PIGuard, a new prompt guard model trained with a novel data-centric training strategy called Mitigating Over-defense for Free (MOF) that reduces trigger-word bias by curating and augmenting training data rather than adding inference-time cost. Evaluates on malicious accuracy (PINT, BIPIA), benign accuracy (PINT, WildGuard) and the new over-defense dimension (NotInject), showing PIGuard achieves state-of-the-art performance across all three simultaneously, outperforming the previous best open-source model by roughly 30 percentage points in average accuracy while remaining fully open-source. Matters as both a named diagnostic benchmark (NotInject) exposing a systemic weakness in prompt-injection detectors and a named, validated ingestion-stage detection defense (PIGuard/MOF) that directly fixes it.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces NotInject, a 339-sample over-defense evaluation dataset built from trigger words common in prompt injection attacks embedded in benign contexts (divided by trigger-word density); evaluates malicious accuracy using PINT and BIPIA benchmark attack data, benign accuracy using PINT and WildGuard benign data, and constructs an open-source training dataset combining existing malicious/benign corpora (e.g., Alpaca) with data-centric augmentation.

source_title: Defending Against Prompt Injection With a Few DefensiveTokens
baselines_compared: Test-time defenses (Reminder, Sandwich, and a heuristic embedding-search baseline analogous to DefensiveToken but using discrete rather than optimized soft tokens) and training-time defenses (StruQ with LoRA and full fine-tuning, SecAlign with LoRA), all evaluated on the same five prompt-injection benchmarks and utility metrics.
key_result: On the largest benchmark (>31K samples), DefensiveToken reduces attack success rate to 0.24% averaged across four models, comparable to training-time defenses (0.20-0.51% ASR) and far below test-time baselines (over 11% ASR); against GCG optimization-based injection it lowers average ASR from 95.2% to 48.8%, versus about 70% ASR (with significant utility loss) for the strongest test-time baseline; on the InjecAgent agentic tool-calling benchmark it reduces average ASR 5x versus 2x for the best test-time baseline, all while imposing smaller utility loss than any baseline and allowing developers to skip the tokens entirely when utility is prioritized.
technical_summary: Proposes DefensiveToken, a test-time prompt-injection defense that inserts a small number (5, recommended) of newly added special tokens with embeddings optimized via a defensive instruction-tuning loss, similar to prompt tuning, so a system developer can prepend them before an LLM call to gain training-time-level security while retaining the option to drop them entirely and recover unmodified state-of-the-art utility when security is not a priority. Evaluates on four 7B/8B open-weight LLMs across five prompt-injection benchmarks spanning manually-designed, optimization-based (GCG), and agentic tool-calling attacks, and against both test-time and training-time defense baselines. Shows DefensiveToken approaches the security of full fine-tuning defenses like StruQ/SecAlign while imposing far less utility cost than any tested baseline, and vastly outperforms other test-time defenses. Matters as a lightweight, flexible defense that narrows the security-utility gap between prompting-based and fine-tuning-based prompt-injection defenses without requiring separate model deployments for secure versus high-utility use cases.
datasets_benchmarks: Cleaned Alpaca instruction-tuning dataset for training; AlpacaFarm and AlpacaEval2 (GPT-4o judge) for utility; five prompt injection security benchmarks including a >31K-sample manually-designed injection benchmark, the SEP benchmark (9.1K instruction/data/injection triples), GCG-based optimization attacks, and the InjecAgent agentic API-calling prompt injection benchmark.

source_title: Discerning and Resolving Knowledge Conflicts through Adaptive Decoding with Contextual Information-Entropy Constraint
baselines_compared: Regular (greedy) decoding; Self-Consistency (Wang et al. 2023b, 40 samples); Contrastive Decoding (Li et al. 2023b); Context-Aware Decoding (Shi et al. 2023a). All baselines reproduced by the authors rather than quoted.
key_result: COIECD improves over regular decoding on every realistic dataset while prior conflict-resolution decoders degrade on non-conflicting data: on NQ it gains EM +0.94/F1 +1.38 (LLaMA2-13B), +10.33 EM/+14.52 F1 (OPT-6.7B) and +2.84 EM/+1.67 F1 (FLAN-T5-3B), where contrastive decoding and context-aware decoding lose 8.38 and 7.09 EM respectively on FLAN-T5-3B. The claimed contribution is robustness across the conflict/non-conflict mix, not peak counterfactual accuracy.
technical_summary: Proposes COIECD, an adaptive decoding rule that first discerns whether a knowledge conflict is actually present before intervening. Frames the token-level decision via an information-entropy constraint: tokens whose contextual information content falls outside a stable-entropy band are treated as conflict points and decoded with a context-favoring objective, while non-conflict tokens fall through to regular decoding. Evaluates on NQ, SQuAD, StrategyQA and Counterfacts across LLaMA2, OPT and FLAN-T5 against Regular, SC, CD and CAD. Shows the central empirical point that existing conflict-solving decoders buy faithfulness on conflicting context at a real accuracy cost on non-conflicting context, which the adaptive gate avoids.
datasets_benchmarks: NaturalQuestions; SQuAD 1.1; StrategyQA (each split post-hoc into conflicting vs non-conflicting subsets rather than synthetically perturbed); Counterfacts (Longpre et al. 2021, fully synthetic conflicts)
